rows.statement: When a btrfs filesystem has no unallocated device space left, the kernel keeps every metadata reservation inside the free space of already allocated metadata chunks, so metadata ENOSPC can occur while data block groups still show free space; read Device unallocated before anything else.

rows.statement: Global reserve in btrfs filesystem usage is metadata held back for emergency work such as deleting files on a full filesystem; it is not free space, and the v7.2 kernel caps its size at 512 MiB (S156 line 394).
rows.quote: Global reserve* -- portion of metadata currently used for global

rows.statement: A balance with a usage filter such as -dusage=N relocates only block groups under N percent used and returns the emptied chunks to unallocated space; usage=0 frees empty block groups without new work space. It is an operator write, never run by the lane.
rows.quote: Balances only block groups with usage under the given percentage

rows.statement: On a single-device btrfs filesystem metadata defaults to the DUP profile, so every metadata byte occupies two bytes of raw device space; this host reports Metadata ratio 2.00 and metadata disk_total about twice metadata total_bytes.
rows.quote: Default on a single device filesystem is *DUP* and is recommended for metadata

rows.statement: The per-type bg_reclaim_threshold file sets a percentage of block-group size: in the v7.2 periodic sweep a block group whose used bytes fall below that percentage is reclaimed whole; this host reads 0 for metadata at capture line 45, so that sweep marks none (S159 lines 2111-2117, 2154-2155).
rows.quote: permanently unusable space) to reclaim the block group.

rows.statement: Per-filesystem space accounting is readable without root under /sys/fs/btrfs/UUID/allocation (singular on kernel 7.2.11, although the btrfs-progs v7.1 chapter heading spells allocations): the kernel attribute list holds global_rsv_reserved and global_rsv_size, beside the data, metadata and system subdirectories.

A snapshot shares its source extents, so deleting files from the original returns no space while any snapshot still references them; on a full filesystem, deleting those snapshots is what returns the space, and deleting files alone cannot (S157 lines 39-41 and 202-206).
